title: The hen on her eggs
hook: Ananda: keep practice warm like a hen on her eggs, and the chicks break out

segments.voice: Yesterday: eleven doors, each opened by seeing clearly. Your line: any door, opened with clear seeing.

The Sakyans of Kapilavatthu, the Buddha's own people, have built a brand-new assembly hall. Nobody has used it yet. They ask the Buddha to be the first, to bless it with a teaching. He comes, and teaches late into the night. Then his back begins to ache. So he asks Ananda to go on teaching, and lies down on his right side, mindful, to rest. Ananda, with the Buddha listening, takes the floor.
screen: `A NEW HALL IN KAPILAVATTHU.` → `THE BUDDHA'S BACK ACHES.` → `ANANDA TAKES THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-third discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, on the disciple in training. Ananda speaks to Mahanama, a Sakyan noble, about someone who isn't finished yet but is on the way. They keep the precepts and guard the senses. They eat in moderation and stay wakeful for practice. They have faith, conscience, care, learning, energy, mindfulness and wisdom. And they can reach the four deep absorptions when they wish. Then Ananda gives a picture from any farmyard. A hen has eight or ten or twelve eggs. She sits on them properly, keeps them warm, broods them well. She doesn't have to wish: oh, may my chicks break out of their shells with their claws and beaks. If she keeps sitting, they will break out safely, on their own. So it is, Ananda says, with someone who keeps these qualities warm. They're able to break through. The hen doesn't push the chicks or crack the shells for them. She doesn't lie awake worrying about hatching. Her whole job is to stay on the eggs. Breaking out is the eggs' business. The same picture appears in another discourse, where the Buddha himself uses it. And when Ananda finishes, the Buddha sits up and says: good, Ananda, good. You've taught the disciple in training well. You can't force the breakthrough. You can keep the practice warm, day after day, and trust what warmth does.
screen: `THE DISCIPLE IN TRAINING` · `PRECEPTS, SENSES, FOOD, WAKEFULNESS` · `A HEN SITS ON HER EGGS` · `THE CHICKS BREAK OUT ON THEIR OWN` · then, large: `THE HEN ON THE EGGS.`

segments.voice: Stay with the breath the way a hen stays on her eggs, holding warm whatever practice you keep on this path: this sit, a kindness, a precept, an honest word. Don't check for results or wish for hatching. Each time the mind wanders off to ask whether this is working, come back and settle on the eggs again.
Ananda. The monk who taught that night, with a picture of practice: keep it warm and steady, and what's ready to break out will break out.
Your line: the hen on the eggs. Warmth, kept up, does its own work. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers use the hen simile to encourage steady, patient daily practice without straining for results; in MN 53 a senior disciple teaches while the Buddha rests and listens.

what a scholar hears: the hen simile appears in more than one discourse, including MN 16, where the Buddha uses it of a monk who has cleared away the mind's barriers and shackles and so is able to break through.

chat.says: I've meditated for months and nothing's happening. Should I push harder?
options: Like Ananda's hen: keep the practice warm, and breaking through comes in its time.
Yes; the hen has to crack the shells herself or the chicks won't hatch.
If nothing's happened by now, it's a sign to give the practice up.
chat.meaning: In MN 53 the hen doesn't wish or force; if she keeps sitting, the chicks break out on their own. Keep the qualities warm, and breakthrough follows.
